article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or abandon a solution
description: The checklist's activities focus on iterative learning rather than a one-way march through phases. Teams may complete a phase multiple times, move backwards to a previous phase, or abandon a solution altogether based on what they learn. This principle frames evidence building as a cyclical design process in which findings at any phase can send teams back to earlier design work.
requirements: Teams must be willing to revisit or repeat phases based on evidence gathered
constraints: Iteration may mean abandoning a solution altogether
target_learners: students in a priority community
target_learning_goals: designing and refining solutions through iterative evidence building
examples: The checklist explicitly states that iterative learning may mean completing a phase multiple times or moving backwards to a previous phase

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring for Structure Strategy (ITSS)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, April). Web-based Intelligent Tutoring for the Structure Strategy (ITSS). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Faded recall sequence within ITSS exercises: scaffolded summaries progress to unsupported recall
description: ITSS exercises follow a recurring multi-step sequence: read nonfiction text, identify the top-level text structure, select signaling words, write a main-idea sentence, generate a thorough summary with comprehension tools, and finally write a recall summary. Scaffolding fades across lessons: "In early lessons, students recall and summarize the text while having access to their (or the I.T.'s) main idea summaries from steps 4 or 5. Later practice lessons remove this aid, and students monitor their recall using the structure strategy." Passages also become more difficult as students complete the exercises.
requirements: The Intelligent Tutor provides feedback after each step; after several unsuccessful attempts it offers hints and a model summary that students may not copy.
constraints: In fourth-grade classrooms in the 2012 study, the recall task was removed after the first month because students had difficulty typing.
target_learners: Students in grades K-8 using ITSS during English language arts
target_learning_goals: Identifying text structure, signaling words, main ideas, and summarizing and recalling factual text
examples: Exercises use passages from science, social studies, sports, and current events; some lessons ask students to write titles, compose their own texts, or correct a fictitious student's muddled use of the strategy.

article_title: Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science
citation: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789v1
title: Keep the randomised intention-to-treat contrast as the causal centre, using engagement analytics only to generate hypotheses
description: In rapid evaluations of educational AI, platform analytics are immediate and granular, but the article argues that "analysis of post-randomisation usage does not provide causal inference". The randomised intention-to-treat contrast should remain the causal centre of the evidence, with engagement data used to generate hypotheses for subsequent tests. This disciplined limit on interpretation lets rapid cycles stay credible while still exploiting granular usage data.
requirements: Random allocation preserving an intention-to-treat contrast as the primary analysis
Engagement analyses reported as associational, adjusted for baseline attainment
constraints: Post-randomisation engagement may reflect motivation, access, prior capability or other characteristics, so it cannot support causal dose-response claims without an identification strategy such as randomised encouragement
target_learners: Secondary school students in mainstream English schools
target_learning_goals: GCSE science attainment in extended written answers
examples: In the Medly evaluation, the intention-to-treat analysis was confirmatory while the questions-answered association and threshold estimates were labelled exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

article_title: Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study
citation: Calvin Isley, Joshua Gilbert, Evangelos Kassos, Michaela Kocher, Allen Nie, Emma Brunskill, Ben Domingue, Jake Hofman, Joscha Legewie, Teddy Svoronos, Charlotte Tuminelli, Sharad Goel. (2025). Assessing the Quality of AI-Generated Exams: A Large-Scale Field Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08314
title: Iterative LLM refinement strategy for generating course-tailored exam questions
description: A two-stage generation procedure, similar to Self-Refine, in which an LLM generator produces multiple-choice questions from instructor-provided course materials and an AI judge labels each question "good" or "bad"; labeled questions are fed back into the generator's prompt as few-shot examples, and the loop repeats until 20 judge-approved questions exist. A final judging round assesses difficulty, appropriateness, and answer correctness, and the 10 hardest approved questions become the class-specific exam. All generation and judging used OpenAI's o3-mini model, with five 2012 AP Statistics practice questions as "good" examples in every prompt.
requirements: Instructor-provided course materials (course description, syllabus, prior homework or exams) converted to plain text as context for both generator and judge
An AI judge applying appropriateness criteria such as no syllabus-logistics questions, mentally solvable calculations, and no duplicated concepts
constraints: Question generation was limited to multiple-choice questions solvable in about 1-2 minutes each
If final judging removed more than 10 questions, an additional 20 questions had to be generated and the full group of 40 re-evaluated
target_learners: college students in STEM and quantitative courses
target_learning_goals: assessment of course-specific conceptual understanding
examples: For each class the loop ran until 20 judge-labeled good questions were generated; a rejected 'bad' biochemistry question tested knowledge of class logistics rather than substantive content

article_title: Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges
citation: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906
title: Deploy ITSs as human-guided instructional resources with teacher mediation, not as autonomous replacements for teachers
description: The review concludes that "ITSs should function as human-guided instructional resources rather than autonomous replacements for teachers". Teachers interpret system-generated evidence against curricular goals, classroom observations, and knowledge of individual learners, because algorithmic recommendations may not reliably distinguish misconceptions, linguistic difficulties, disengagement, and technical interruptions. AI analytics should function as an additional source of formative evidence rather than an authoritative replacement for teachers' professional knowledge.
requirements: Teacher preparedness, pedagogical and curricular alignment, valid assessment, and teachers' capacity to translate system outputs into meaningful instructional action.
constraints: The review states algorithmic classifications may misrepresent learners when models are trained on unrepresentative data or rely on narrow indicators of mathematical competence.
target_learners: mathematics learners in classrooms where teachers mediate ITS use
target_learning_goals: formative assessment, targeted intervention, and differentiated mathematics instruction
examples: The review's synthesis found the most consistent benefits when systems combined valid learner modelling with adaptive tasks, diagnostic feedback, calibrated scaffolding, and meaningful teacher mediation.
key_sources: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906

article_title: From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education
citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: ITAS conversational instructor analytics agent
description: A single-agent conversational analytics system that lets instructors interrogate deployment data through natural language while preserving student privacy. The agent "queries pre-aggregated BigQuery summaries, assembles results with lesson metadata, and produces a natural language response", narrating pre-queried data without writing SQL or performing calculations. It cross-references video seek data, code execution logs, and checkpoint submissions to surface aggregate pedagogical patterns, never returning individual transcripts or identifiable interaction logs. The narrow-scope design applies the same reliability principle as the teaching architecture.
requirements: Pre-aggregated BigQuery summaries and lesson metadata must exist for the agent to narrate
constraints: The agent never writes SQL or performs calculations, and never returns individual transcripts or identifiable interaction logs
target_learners: instructors of quantum computing courses
content developers
target_learning_goals: instructor awareness of aggregate pedagogical patterns such as engagement gaps and failure types
examples: In the pilot, the agent surfaced the Module 2 dead zone finding without an explicit instructor query and distinguished a reading comprehension error from a genuine conceptual gap

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Iteration branch of the taxonomy: seven categories of loop difficulties
description: The iteration branch classifies difficulties with loops into seven categories: the repeating nature of iteration statements, interaction with code outside the loop, order of execution of loop parts, state (including control-variable difficulties), difficulties with the loop condition, nesting, and break and continue. Examples include the "loop is if" belief and thinking nested loops execute simultaneously. The branch draws on both cited literature and the authors' own interview and test data.
requirements: Applies to conceptual difficulties in reading iteration statements; the loop is described as consisting of four parts: initialization, condition check, body, and update of control variable
constraints: Some entries, such as struggling to identify ranges from relational operators, are noted by the authors as possibly lexical difficulties but kept for their conceptual component
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding loops, loop conditions, control variables, and nested iteration
examples: The break and continue category records beliefs such as "break is continue" and thinking break terminates the whole program

article_title: Comprehensive Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882
title: Four-component architecture of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Domain Model, Student Model, Tutor Model, and User Interface
description: The review describes the four-component architecture as "a widely accepted framework for defining ITS". The Domain Model encapsulates concepts, rules, and problem-solving strategies as an expert knowledge base for assessing performance and identifying errors. The Student Model continuously monitors learners' progress, adapting to cognitive and affective states, often refined with Bayesian networks, ML algorithms, and data mining. The Tutor Model determines instructional strategies and when and how to intervene, while the User Interface facilitates student-system communication using human-computer interaction principles.
requirements: Requires a Domain Model representing the subject matter so student input can be compared against expert knowledge for accurate feedback
Requires a Student Model continuously updated from learner interactions to predict student needs and learning paths
target_learners: Learners in traditional classrooms and online learning platforms
Distance learners and students in large classrooms
target_learning_goals: Individualized instruction and personalized feedback across subject domains
Real-time feedback and adaptation to varied learning paces
examples: The review illustrates the architecture with Figure 1, citing [62], and notes methods such as Bayesian networks and ML algorithms are employed to refine the Student Model's accuracy
key_sources: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882

article_title: Comprehensive Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882
title: Taxonomy of pedagogical strategies in ITS: rule-based/expert systems, case-based reasoning, and cognitive tutors, grounded in established learning theories
description: The review organizes ITS pedagogical strategies into rule-based and expert systems using if-then rules and knowledge bases, case-based reasoning systems matching current learner situations to stored past cases, and cognitive tutors providing step-by-step guidance based on cognitive models of knowledge acquisition. It states these strategies "are often implemented using rule-based systems, expert systems, case-based reasoning, and cognitive tutors". The review also links designs to learning theories: constructivist theory supports exploratory and problem-based scenarios, Self-Regulated Learning theory is reflected in learner modeling and formative feedback, and Cognitive Load Theory guides task complexity adjustment and stepwise hints.
requirements: CBR success depends on the quality and relevance of stored cases
Accurate cognitive models for cognitive tutors require extensive domain expertise and iterative refinement
constraints: Rule-based and expert systems can be complex to develop and maintain for domains with many rules
Cognitive tutors can be resource-intensive and their effectiveness varies by implementation and context
CBR systems can become computationally intensive when retrieving cases from large datasets
target_learners: Students in domains such as mathematics, programming, physics, and medical diagnosis
target_learning_goals: Individualized problem-solving support
Personalized instruction and feedback adapted to learner responses
examples: Named systems include GUIDON and the LISP Tutor for medical diagnosis, AutoTutor, CBR-Tutor, CBR-Works, Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor, ACT-R Tutors, SQL-Tutor, Andes Physics Tutor, and Electronix Tutor

citation: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882
title: Systematic review corpus of 127 included ITS studies selected via PRISMA from 37,617 initial records
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus assembled through a Kitchenham-style systematic literature search across Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Springer. The selection process states that "37,617 articles were initially identified, 9,485 were eliminated after deduplication, 2,112 were excluded after screening titles and abstracts, and finally, 127 articles were included for full review, supplemented by 26 reports from specialized web sources". Inclusion criteria required evaluation of educational effectiveness in real learning environments, empirical data, validation of 6 weeks or more, samples of 100 or more participants, and peer-reviewed English-language papers.

article_title: Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics
citation: Sibley, L., Berner, T., & Schmalfeldt, T. (2026). Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics. Computers and Education Open 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100420
title: Intelligent tutoring systems as three-model architectures operationalizing formative assessment
description: The article describes ITS as autonomous technologies that continuously assess learners' progress through formative assessment and deliver tailored instructional support. It states that "ITS typically consist of three core components: a domain model (representing the knowledge to be learned), a student model (tracking individual learning progress and misconceptions), and a tutoring model (or pedagogical module) that determines what instructional support to provide". Based on these models, ITS provide individualized support such as hints and error-specific feedback and adapt task sequencing to ensure mastery before progression. In this study the architecture was implemented in a CTAT+TutorShop tutor with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing driving task selection.
requirements: A diagnostic engine enabling real-time adaptations based on students' responses, integrating learner modeling, adaptive task sequencing, and dynamic feedback mechanisms
constraints: The article notes ITS cannot fully replace the pedagogical sensitivity of human teachers
target_learners: second-grade primary school students
target_learning_goals: second-grade mathematics: addition and subtraction with and without carrying or borrowing
examples: The study's tutor covered 13 arithmetic skills with increasing complexity, used graduated spoken-audio hints, and selected tasks via the Sequential Mastery Learning – Easier First algorithm based on BKT mastery estimates

It reports ITSs have been shown to be effective in STEM subjects and are used in biology, bioinformatics, and other STEM courses.

article_title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Kulik, J. A., & Fletcher, J. D. (2016). Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315581420
title: Defining features of intelligent tutoring systems: knowledge structures plus inner- and outer-loop tutoring behaviors
description: The review distinguishes intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) from earlier CAI tutors structurally and behaviorally. Structurally, ITSs combine an explicit domain-knowledge model, a dynamic student model, a pedagogical module, and a user interface, drawing hints and feedback from "organized knowledge databases, or information structures". Behaviorally, following VanLehn, "ITSs display both inner- and outer-loop behaviors, whereas CAI tutors display outer-loop behaviors only": inner-loop support (prompting, hinting) occurs while the student works on a problem, outer-loop support (feedback, new problems) at end of problem. The meta-analysis used expert classification plus the during-problem-help criterion to identify ITSs.
requirements: The article treats helping learners while they work on a problem, not just after solutions are recorded, as a practical criterion for classifying a tutor as an ITS.
target_learners: learners in K-12, postsecondary, and military training settings evaluated in ITS studies
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge and problem-solving skills taught by intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The 50 evaluated systems ranged from Cognitive Tutor and the DARPA Digital Tutor to Sherlock 2, AutoTutor, and KERMIT, all classified as step-based or substep-based ITSs.

article_title: Serial-order short-term memory predicts vocabulary development: Evidence from a longitudinal study.
citation: Leclercq, A.-L., & Majerus, S. (2010). Serial Order Short-Term Memory Predicts Vocabulary Development: Evidence from a Longitudinal Study. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018540
title: Item-order distinction in verbal STM and the serial-order account of vocabulary acquisition
description: The article organizes verbal short-term memory into two dissociable components: order information, "the sequential order in which the items are presented", and item information, the phonological, lexical and semantic characteristics of an item. Recent STM models store these in separate but interconnected systems, with a specialized system encoding sequential order and item information represented via temporary activation in the language network. Following Gupta, the authors propose that lexical acquisition and verbal STM capacity are driven by the same serial-order system, which replays activated language representations in correct order, reinforcing newly created lexical representations. The study's longitudinal dissociation — serial order STM, not item STM, predicting vocabulary — is offered as support for this account.
requirements: Tasks must independently maximize serial order versus item retention demands, as the animal race and single nonword delayed repetition tasks were designed to do
constraints: The account is tested here for children aged 4 to 5; the authors note item STM could be a stronger determinant at earlier developmental stages where phonological representation accuracy constrains vocabulary growth
A third, non-controlled ability such as selective attention to serial order or sequential rehearsal might mediate the observed longitudinal relationship
target_learners: typically developing kindergarten children aged 4-5 years
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
new phonological word-form learning
examples: The serial order reconstruction task presented sequences of seven highly familiar monosyllabic animal names and had children rearrange cards on a staircase, minimizing item demands
The castle task required delayed repetition of single monosyllabic nonwords with low-familiarity diphones while repeating 'bla' during retention to prevent rehearsal
key_sources: Leclercq, A.-L., & Majerus, S. (2010). Serial Order Short-Term Memory Predicts Vocabulary Development: Evidence from a Longitudinal Study. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018540

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Iterative data-driven validation pattern: create, test, revise from performance and feedback, and retest until gameplay statistically matches external criteria
description: This design pattern structures assessment-game development as repeated cycles in which the game is created, tested with students, revised based on logged performance and user feedback, and retested until gameplay is statistically matched to independent ratings of the target skill. The article states it "utilized an iterative data-driven validation process in which the game was created, tested, revised based on student performance and feedback, and retested." Two iterative evaluations with third- and fourth-graders refined dialogue choices, verified challenge difficulty, and produced the scoring algorithms.
requirements: Student testing sessions with observers recording attention, areas of difficulty, and reactions
Game logs tracking the location and time of each mouse click
An independent external measure of the target skill for validation
constraints: The article notes the appropriate level of difficulty to obtain useful response variability was not evident a priori and had to be established from captured gameplay
target_learners: elementary school students (third and fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of social skills within an engaging game

citation: Létourneau, A., Martineau, M. D., Charland, P., Karran, J. A., Boasen, J. & Léger, P. M. (2025). A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education. npj Science of Learning 10:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00320-7
title: Core components of effective ITS deployment: personalization, adaptivity, and immediate data-driven feedback
description: The review synthesizes the features that distinguish successful ITS deployments. It concludes that "personalization and adaptivity appear to be part of a core of ITS components, which influence their effectiveness": systems tailoring content to individual needs, prior knowledge and learning styles, and providing immediate, real-time data-driven feedback during tasks. Integrated, these components break complex concepts into individualized manageable steps and supply just-in-time hints, potentially improving engagement and retention. The synthesis draws on studies of Yixue, UZWEBMAT, Rimac and TECH8.

Tailoring of instructional content to individual student needs, prior knowledge, and learning styles

target_learning_goals: Subject-matter learning and performance, primarily in STEM subjects and language learning

description: The third principle for success: "Successful projects iterate within each phase until meeting the milestones to a high standard, set flexible timelines and budgets, and adapt their plan in response to new information." title: ITAP: data-driven hint generation via state abstraction, path construction, and state reification
description: ITAP (Intelligent Teaching Assistant for Programming) is a self-improving data-driven tutoring system that generates personalized next-step hints for code-writing problems. It combines algorithms for "state abstraction, path construction, and state reification to fully automate the process of hint generation", building a solution space graph from student states and constructing paths even for never-seen states. It requires only a reference solution and an automatic test method, and updates the solution space every time a student attempts a solution.

A test method that can automatically score code (e.g. pairs of expected input and output)

target_learning_goals: Writing correct Python code for code-writing problems
Moving from incorrect program states to correct solutions via next-step hints

title: Immersive Technology Evaluation Measure (ITEM) five-domain framework for user experience of immersive technology in medical education
description: The ITEM is a validated instrument developed to capture the user experience of immersive technology in medical education, organized into five domains: "immersion, motivation, cognitive load, system usability, and debriefing." constraints: The authors note the ITEM framework used for data analysis might have restricted the focus to responses within its scope, suggesting an inductive approach for future exploration

health professions education learners

examples: The study applied the five ITEM domains as predefined themes in deductive thematic analysis of 11 interview transcripts, with subthemes emerging within each domain

title: Implicit Theories of Emotional Intelligence Scale (ITEIS)
description: The ITEIS is a 12-item self-report scale, adapted by Costa and Faria (2020a) from Dweck's (1999) theorisation, evaluating individuals' implicit theories about the malleability of emotional intelligence for the Portuguese secondary school context. "The ITEIS includes a total of 12 items rated on a 6-point Likert-type scale", with six incremental items and six entity items. citation: Casper Anne M., Eddy Sarah L., Freeman Scott. (2019). True Grit: Passion and persistence make an innovative course design work. PLoS Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000359
title: Adapt evidence-based course designs to your student population through iterative, data-driven experimentation rather than one-shot adoption
description: The article argues faculty should adopt evidence-based teaching the way researchers adopt new lab techniques: "follow the literature closely, get initial training from experienced practitioners, start with limited trials, be prepared for disappointing results at first, engage with colleagues who can provide feedback and advice, and be willing to make changes." The first author ran three hypothesis-driven iterations, using outcome data (exam scores, DFW rates) after each to diagnose why the design failed and what to change, ultimately succeeding on the third attempt.
requirements: Willingness to collect and analyze outcome data after each implementation
Time, institutional support, mentoring, and in-person learning from experienced instructors before major changes
Perseverance after initial failures, which the article notes one-third of faculty lack
constraints: The article states adopting evidence-based practices is challenging for STEM faculty who identify primarily as bench- or field-based researchers, and that fidelity of implementation requires sustained effort
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment STEM courses
target_learning_goals: improved exam performance and reduced failure rates in introductory STEM courses
examples: After experiment 2's null result, the author changed preclass preparation from reading assignments and online quizzes to instructor-made 15-minute video lectures plus in-class prep quizzes, motivated by EMU students' lower reading-comprehension percentile

article_title: Fixed or mixed: a comparison of three, four and mixed-option multiple-choice tests in a Fetal Surveillance Education Program.
citation: Zoanetti N, Beaves M, Griffin P, Wallace E M. (2013). Fixed or mixed: a comparison of three, four and mixed-option multiple-choice tests in a Fetal Surveillance Education Program. BMC Medical Education 13:35. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-35
title: Decide the number of multiple-choice response options at the item level, on psychometric and educational grounds, rather than by a uniform policy
description: The article argues that decisions about the number of MCQ response options should be made item by item: "decisions about the number of response options be made at the item level, with plausible options being added to complete each item on both psychometric and educational grounds rather than complying with a uniform policy." The mixed-option form outperformed fixed-option forms, and item-level variation was considerable, so rigid adherence to a fixed option number is counter-productive. Educationally important alternatives should be retained even with low selection frequencies.
requirements: Item analysis data from prior test administrations to identify functioning and non-functioning options
Subject-matter expert judgement to identify educationally or clinically important alternatives
constraints: The approach is post-hoc: options removed were non-functioning, which differs from writing only three options from the start
Caution is needed with positive-discrimination criteria when respondent numbers in low-response categories are small
Results derive from one FSEP item bank; generalisation to other contexts is not known
target_learners: medical practitioners in obstetric fetal surveillance training
target_learning_goals: assessment of fetal surveillance knowledge and clinical decision-making
examples: In the FSEP, the mixed-option test form retaining the best-performing version of each item became the preferred test format
Item writers are advised to write only educationally important and plausible options until a minimum of three are produced, adding more only if immediately forthcoming
